articles.title: John Mulaney Circling Lead Role in ‘Get Smart’ Reboot at Warner Bros.
articles.summary: John Mulaney is circling the role of Agent Maxwell Smart in Warner Bros. upcoming movie reboot of “Get Smart,” Variety has confirmed. The project is still in very early stages. Seth Grahame-Smith, who wrote 2025’s “Now You See Me: Now You Don’t,” is set to pen the screenplay.
body: Mulaney’s most recent starring role was as the host of Netflix’s anti-talk show “Everybody’s Live with John Mulaney,” which had a 12-episode run in 2025. He has a nine-show New York comedy tour, “Mulaney Takes Manhattan,” set to kick off in January. His next movie role will be in David O. Russell’s sports biopic “Madden” as Trip Hawkins, the founder of the video game giant Electronic Arts.

Mulaney joked during the 2024 Governors Awards that he auditioned for the role of “Young Cop” in Maggie Gyllenhaal’s “The Bride!,” which was a Warner Bros. release. Now it looks like the four-time Emmy winner and WB. are finally coming together.

articles.title: Company review – Casey Affleck entertains us with creepy campfire tales
articles.summary: Venice film festival: Affleck’s third film as a director is a diverting gothic anthology about mysterious strangers, murder and – pointedly – wronged men. Gather ye ’round the glowing screen for a Casey Affleck campfire tale. It contains superstitions and murder and human oddities of all stripes.
body: Actually there is much to relish in Company, Affleck’s third film as a director, even if many of its elements feel like off-the-peg eccentricities; a little too laundered and self-consciously strange. It begins in tried and tested fashion with the arrival of a mysterious stranger on a dark winter’s night. The stranger takes a seat and spins a tale, at which point December 1975 melts into 1953, then 1903, before finally the film crosses the ocean to Europe at the tail end of the plague. Nick Nolte is a hermit pining for his lost daughter, while Ben Mendelsohn plays a mean, mordant farmer who reaches for his handgun too readily. Both men, one suspects, are destined for a bloody end.

articles.title: Netflix Orders New Series Take On ‘Lonesome Dove’ From ‘East of Eden’ Showrunners Zoe Kazan and Jeb Stuart
articles.summary: “Lonesome Dove,” which was originally adapted into an Emmy- and Golden Globe-winning CBS miniseries starring Robert Duvall in 1989, is getting a new take at Netflix. The streamer announced Tuesday that it had ordered “Lonesome Dove” to series, from co-showrunners Zoe Kazan and Jeb Stuart.
body: Teton Ridge acquired the rights to “Lonesome Dove” last year; at the time, it announced that development would begin with the first book in the series, “Lonesome Dove,” followed by the rest of the tetralogy, including “Streets of Laredo,” “Dead Man’s Walk” and “Comanche Moon.” The novels focus on members of the Texas Ranger Division, spanning from when Texas was a republic until the start of the 20th century when it was part of the U.S.

Kazan and Stuart will serve as co-showrunners/writers/executive producers, while EPs also include Thomas Tull, Jillian Share and Jen Gorton of Teton Ridge Entertainment; Jon Jashni; Diana Ossana; and Curtis McMurtry of the McMurtry Estate. Diana Ossana, McMurty’s longtime creative partner, is also an exec producer.

articles.title: Telluride Takeaways: From Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti’s ‘Debut’ to Nathan Fielder’s Audacious Dare to the Doc Branch
articles.summary: On my last morning in Telluride, halfway through breakfast at Butcher & Baker, Kenneth Branagh stopped at the table on his way to a Q&A for “Into the Breach,” the National Theatre documentary he produced. He had a story.
body: That’s the festival. The Telluriders have gone home, Venice wraps in a few days and we came down the mountain knowing more about this Oscar race than we did going up. Christopher Nolan’s mythological epic “The Odyssey” is still the one to beat. It won’t be a cakewalk. Here’s what else I carried down.
“ The Debut ” handed Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti their moment.

Jesse Eisenberg’s third feature behind the camera premiered Saturday night. By the next day, it was the hottest ticket in town. “The Debut” drops Moore’s Mona, a meek suburban homemaker who lands a bit part in a community theater musical, into the front of the best actress race. It’s the funniest, warmest thing she’s done in years. Giamatti, whom Eisenberg calls his “favorite actor,” plays the tyrant director shaping her. During one rehearsal scene between them — a master-class, no other word for it — the Telluride crowd applauded in the middle of the movie. You rarely see that happen once at a festival. It happened again before the credits.

articles.title: Congress Begins Drafting 20% Federal Film Incentive With Trump’s Blessing (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: Members of Congress are drafting legislation that would create a 20% federal film and TV incentive — with bonuses that could bring it as high as 30% — after President Trump endorsed the idea last week. The bill is expected to be introduced this month, and perhaps as soon as the end of next week,
body: For the last year, the Motion Picture Association and entertainment unions have been advocating for an incentive that would compete with generous subsidies from the U.K., Canada, Australia and scores of other countries. Trump threw his weight behind the idea in a Truth Social post on Aug. 31, a development expected to unlock Republican support on Capitol Hill.

The draft legislation broadly aligns with the MPA’s request. The bill would offer a base credit of 20% of all labor costs, both below-the-line and above-the-line. A wide range of productions would be eligible, including reality TV and animation in addition to films and scripted TV shows, according to sources familiar with the legislation. It would not include news or sports broadcasts.

Producers could claim up to two of those uplifts, for a maximum of 30%. The federal tax credit would stack on top of state incentives, meaning that productions could see a total subsidy of 60% or more depending on where they film.

articles.title: Bunker review – Cruz and Bardem just can’t dig Florian Zeller’s shallow thriller out of a hole
articles.summary: Venice film festival: An architect (Javier Bardem) alienates his book editor wife (Penélope Cruz) when he agrees to build a luxurious bunker for a tech billionaire. Even the formidable pairing of Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem can’t save this new movie from writer-director Florian Zeller – his…
body: Bunker has nothing that interesting or original to say about its metaphorically showcased theme of alienation and inequality; the central relationship is left unexplored in favour of so-so home-invasion suspense styling – although one extended marital-argument scene showed what might have been achieved if their relationship was the film’s point – and the violent finale ending is outrageously glib, silly and unconvincing. An off-camera paramedic or doctor actually has to be heard explaining in a brief sentence afterwards what is supposed to have happened. Very lame.

Cruz and Bardem are Sofia and Miguel, a stylish Spanish couple with two teen daughters; the family has moved to London so that Sofia, a book editor, can take up a job managing a UK publisher’s foreign literature in translation list.

Miguel is a world-famous architect (what other sort is there?) who cordially tells an interviewer that he can work in any city. It seems as if he might himself have designed the huge, modernist rear extension to their handsome Victorian terrace house.

articles.title: Andrew Garfield takes on Sam Altman in creepy first teaser for Artificial
articles.summary: Luca Guadagnino-directed film will be released by Neon after being dropped by Amazon amid OpenAI partnership. Big tech goes to Hollywood: is Silicon Valley ready for a silver-screen reckoning? The first teaser trailer of Luca Guadagnino ’s Artificial has been released.
body: After being dropped by Amazon MGM Studios in June, the biopic of the OpenAI tech executive Sam Altman will be released in the US on 25 December by Neon after it premieres at the New York film festival this October.
In the trailer, Andrew Garfield as Altman walks down the staircase of a luxurious mansion before entering a basement containing dozens of machine guns.
“The future’s inevitable,” says Altman as ominous electronic music plays. “Countries will fall. Industries are gonna collapse. And we get to be the ones to shepherd people into this new world.”

In a statement earlier this summer, Amazon said that it believed “Artificial will be better served if it were released by a different studio and are working closely with the film-making team to find the film a new home”.

articles.title: Glastonbury confirms ticket sale dates - and highest ever price
articles.summary: The festival will return in June after taking a fallow year, but tickets have topped £400 for the first time.
body: After taking a fallow year in 2026, the Glastonbury Festival has confirmed that tickets for next year's event will go on sale in October.
Tickets for the weekend will cost £408 including a £5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of £29.50 from 2025.

Headliners for the festival, which takes place from 23 to 27 June, have yet to be announced, but rumours are already swirling, with everyone from Harry Styles and Fontaines DC to Taylor Swift and Stevie Wonder said to be in the mix.
Tickets for the festival typically sell out in less than an hour, with thousands of fans joining online queues to fight for their place.

articles.title: Practical Magic 2 review – Bullock and Kidman return for odd sequel that still casts a spell
articles.summary: A nostalgia-bait return to the witchy 90s comedy is as strange and messy as the first but there are warm seasonal pleasures to be had. Much has changed in the universe, cosmic and otherwise, since the Owens witches last graced the big screen with their practical magic of sleeping draughts, midnight…
body: Which makes Practical Magic 2, reuniting both Kidman and Bullock, and Stockard Channing and Dianne Wiest as their lovingly eccentric aunts, somewhat of an anomaly, at once a seeming inevitability and, as a matrilineal romance comedy (though decidedly not a romcom) starring two 60-year-old women, an oddity. There’s no circumventing nostalgia bait, but Practical Magic remains so idiosyncratic in tone and, well, kookiness, that a sequel somewhat appeals.

This will prove irksome if you, like me, are timeline-sensitive, but the original’s playful sense of tone, logic and rules in general was admittedly central to its appeal. I find it endearing that the magic in the Practical Magic franchise allows for generational curses, purgatorial spirits and the automatic stirring of coffee cups but not, say, levitating suitcases upstairs, forcing poor Kidman to lug oversized bags through three separate scenes.

articles.title: Oasis' Cardiff reunion gig was 'hugely emotional' say film-makers
articles.summary: Filmmakers describe the gig as a "hugely emotional" experience that took Noel Gallagher by surprise.
body: Will Lovelace and Dylan Southern's portrayal of the band's world tour in 2025 also captured the moment Liam and Noel reunited in the rehearsal studios following a 15-year hiatus.
Reflecting on the opening gig, Southern said: "You saw grown men who probably rarely express their emotions crying and hugging each other.
"Noel says in the film that he completely underestimated what it would be like, and it really did kind of hit him hard."
Lovelace said: "Those opening few moments, just as they're about to go on stage in Cardiff, and then the first song, was definitely a turning point on the tour but certainly in the film."

articles.title: Paramount Argues That the States Post a $1.88 Billion Bond to Cover Warner Bros. Bills
articles.summary: Courts have historically side-eyed issuing massive bonds in merger cases, particularly when the government challenges the deal. The states have stressed that Paramount proposed the term to win over shareholders.
body: Paramount is continuing to press a dozen states led by California and the Writers Guild of America to bear the costs of the hold up caused by their lawsuits challenging the $111 billion megamerger.

The studio has asked for a $1.88 billion bond to cover losses if it wins the cases. In July, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín temporarily halted the deal and scheduled a trial for March, months past its target closing date of late September.

There will be major financial repercussions for the delay. Under the agreement, Warners shareholders are owed roughly $650 million per quarter or $6.9 million per day if the merger hasn’t closed by Oct. 1. The bond represents the maximum payout to investors, plus legal fees.

The states and WGA have pushed back on the demand, arguing that Paramount proposed the fee in a bid to win support from shareholders, who were weighing a rival bid from Netflix at the time. The studio “now wishes to offload that responsibility,” stated a filing from California Attorney General Rob Bonta last month.
